name: Xerj
tagline: A local search engine in one file that indexes your folders so AI agents find answers instead of reading everything.
sentence: Run one command to index a folder of code, documents, or logs, then your AI agent searches the index instead of reading files one by one - finding the right file first try 94% of the time.

visual.alt: The Xerj logo on a dark background: 'XERJ' in large bold white letters with '.AI' in yellow, a horizontal yellow line above, and 'SEARCH FOR THE AGENT ERA' in gray below.
visual.caption: The Xerj branding - a local search engine built for AI agents.

board.say: AI agents that need to search your files read them one by one into their conversation, using up working memory fast. Or they use basic text-matching (like a find-in-files command) and miss what they need.
board.eg: Your agent needs to find how a function is used across a codebase. It reads file after file, burning through its memory budget, and still misses the relevant one.

board.say: You run one command - `xerj autoindex ~/my-project` - and the engine indexes the folder in the background. Then agents search the index instead of reading files.
board.eg: Index a project folder once. The engine detects file types automatically - code, JSON, CSV, PDF, email - and creates the right indexes for each.

board.say: A folder of code, documents, logs, or data files. Supports 13 format families: source code in 36 languages, PDF, spreadsheets, JSON, CSV, email, and more.
board.eg: A checkout of a large open-source project, a folder of PDF research papers, or a directory of server logs.

board.say: It indexes your files and serves search results through a standard interface that AI agents and existing tools already understand.
steps: Detects each file's type automatically and indexes its contents - source code is parsed by structure (using tree-sitter), so function names and definitions are preserved
Offers keyword search, meaning-based search, and a hybrid of both, all from a single search command
Speaks the Elasticsearch query language, so any existing tool, dashboard, or script that queries Elasticsearch works without changes
board.eg: Index an 80-file codebase. The agent searches for 'database connection retry logic' and gets the right file on the first try - versus scrolling through files one by one.

board.say: AI agents that search faster, use less memory, and find the right files without reading everything.

outputs.eg: An AI agent finds the right file on its first search 94% of the time, versus 38% with basic text search
Agents that search the index use 2.7 times fewer output words than agents that read files with find-in-files commands
A built-in memory store lets agents save and recall facts between sessions, with per-agent isolation

before: AI agents that need to search your files read them one by one, filling their working memory and slowing down. A 500-file codebase means hundreds of file reads.
Basic text-matching finds exact strings but misses meaning. Searching for 'retry logic' won't find a function called `exponential_backoff` unless the comment mentions 'retry'.
after: One command indexes the folder. AI agents search the index and get structured results - function definitions, line numbers, and context - without reading every file.
Hybrid search combines keyword matching and meaning, so 'retry logic' finds `exponential_backoff` even without an exact match. The right file comes up first 94% of the time.
uses_note: Xerj is 108 days old. No named real-world adopters could be verified. The project's benchmarks are its own and have not been independently reproduced.

coverage.meta: Automated technical overview of the codebase

steps: Install with one command: `curl -fsSL https://xerj.org/get | sh` (Mac/Linux) or `irm https://xerj.org/get.ps1 | iex` (Windows).
Start the engine and index a folder: `xerj --insecure --data-dir ./data &` then `xerj autoindex ~/some-project`.
Try a search: `curl 'http://localhost:9200/your-index/_search?q=your+query'` or try the [live playground](https://xerj.org/playground/).

If that scan passes: install with `curl -fsSL https://xerj.org/get | sh`, start with `xerj --insecure --data-dir ./data &`, index a folder with `xerj autoindex ~/some-project`, and run a search. 10 minutes max.

footprint.disk: Ships as a single static binary - no Java, no dependencies. Download size not published. The optional neural search mode downloads about 90 MB of model files.
footprint.memory: No data found. Default search mode is lexical (no neural models loaded). Neural mode loads three model files locally.
footprint.runs_on: Mac, Windows, and Linux on x86-64 and arm64. Linux builds are statically linked, so they run on any distribution including Alpine. Built from source with a stable Rust toolchain.

best_for: You work with AI agents that search codebases, document folders, or log archives - Xerj replaces file-by-file reading with indexed search
You want a lightweight local search engine with no Java dependency that speaks the Elasticsearch language - existing tools and dashboards just work
skip_if: You need a production Elasticsearch replacement with full feature coverage - 3 of 1,369 conformance tests fail, and features like scroll cursors behave differently
You want neural (meaning-based) search out of the box - the default mode is keyword-only, and neural mode requires downloading model files and is still opt-in
You need a battle-tested tool - this is 108 days old with no named production users

alternatives.name: Elasticsearch
alternatives.line: The industry standard. Full-featured and production-hardened, but requires Java, more memory, and more setup. Xerj is designed as a lighter local alternative.

alternatives.name: ripgrep
alternatives.line: A fast text search tool. No indexing, no server - just searches files directly. Faster for one-off searches, but does not offer meaning-based search or an agent-friendly interface.

alternatives.name: Meilisearch
alternatives.line: An instant-search engine in a single binary. Focused on user-facing search with typo tolerance. Does not parse source code by structure.

watch: **Young project - 108 days old with no named production users.** The benchmarks are the project's own and have not been independently reproduced. The claim of '40x fewer tokens than grep' in the About section contradicts the body's '2.7x' figure.

**Default mode listens without authentication.** The `--insecure` flag disables all authentication and encryption. Anyone on the network can query, index, and delete data. Authentication is on by default without that flag, but the quickstart guide uses it.

**Optional reranking sends data to an external service.** The Jev reranker (by TypeSafe AI) sends search result text to an external API for re-scoring. It is off by default, but you should know it exists before enabling it.

**Not a drop-in Elasticsearch replacement.** Three conformance tests fail, scroll cursors are bounded snapshots (not infinite streams), and some aggregation features are missing. The project calls itself a 'migration bridge, not a clone.'
